note: A groupId must be verified before publishing: a DNS TXT record for the domain, or the code-hosting account for io.github.*.
The module path is a domain or repository path, so whoever controls the domain or repository controls the name.
A vendor prefix belongs to the first account to publish under it; nobody else can add packages to it.
@scope/ names belong to a user or organisation, but scopes are optional and unscoped names are first come, first served.
One flat namespace. Namespace prefixes (PEP 752) are accepted but not deployed.
One flat namespace. Namespaced crates (RFC 3243) are accepted but not implemented on crates.io.
One flat namespace; prefixes are a naming convention only.
A new name is rejected if it matches any existing project after removing . _ - and folding l/i→1 and o→0 (ultranormalize). Other misspellings pass.
A new name is rejected if it equals an existing one once punctuation is removed (2017). Other misspellings pass.
- and _ are equivalent (canon_crate_name), so such variants cannot be registered. A typosquat check runs after publication and only emails the crates.io team.
A push is rejected if the name equals an established gem's (≥ 10,000 downloads or released in the last five years) ignoring case, _ and -.
A package whose vendor is one edit away from an existing vendor with the same package name is rejected if the existing package has ≥ 1M downloads; otherwise the admins are emailed.
Names are domains and repository paths; there is no registration step.
Names sit under a verified namespace, so confusable names fall under namespace verification.
Every upload gets static and dynamic analysis and a risk score; high scores go to manual review. The team reports finding 70–80% of the malware it removes itself.
Aikido's malware detections are imported and shipped in the metadata Composer reads; Composer 2.10 blocks flagged versions.
Report-driven: trusted researchers (Observers) report through an API, and admins quarantine projects (hidden from the index, frozen) pending review. Auto-quarantine is proposed.
Malicious packages are removed and replaced by a '0.0.1-security' holding package, but npm does not document how they are detected.
Typosquat checks on new crates alert the team; malicious crates are deleted, their accounts disabled and a RustSec advisory published.
The mirror caches whatever a VCS serves; malicious modules are removed on request.
Central validates signatures and metadata on upload but documents no malware analysis; malicious components are removed once reported.
Yank (PEP 592): resolvers skip the release unless it is pinned exactly.
cargo yank: new resolution skips the version; Cargo.lock keeps using it.
A retract directive in a later go.mod hides the version from new resolution; go.mod requirements keep it.
npm deprecate only warns; the version still resolves. Hiding it means unpublishing, which also breaks lockfiles.
Soft deletion removes a version from the metadata Composer resolves, keeps a record and can be undone; lockfiles fetch archives from the forge, which the maintainer controls.
A yank removes the .gem file, so locked installs of it fail.
Nothing can be withdrawn.
Unpublishing is allowed within 72 hours, or later only for packages with no dependents, under 300 weekly downloads and one owner.
Deletion is allowed within 72 hours, or later only for crates with one owner, no dependents and few downloads (RFC 3660).
The mirror and checksum database keep every version; deleting the tag upstream changes nothing.
Released components can never be changed or deleted.
Deletion is now a recoverable soft delete with a public record, but the code lives in the maintainer's repository, which they can delete.
Owners can delete files and releases at any time; only the filename can never be reused.
A yank, possible at any time, deletes the file; only the version number stays taken.
Composer blocks versions with security advisories during update/require by default (policy.advisories.block); installs from a lockfile are not checked.
npm install runs an audit by default and reports known vulnerabilities, but installs them.
pip does not check advisories; pip-audit is separate.
Cargo does not check advisories; cargo-audit (RustSec) is separate.
Bundler does not check advisories; bundler-audit is separate.
The go command does not check advisories; govulncheck is separate.
Maven does not check advisories; plugins such as OWASP Dependency-Check are separate.
